extracted.intended_audience: novelists, fiction-writers, and students/critics of narrative technique
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on selecting and applying narrative method (dramatic/scene-based vs pictorial/narrative) in novels and stories, with principles for showing interior life, using the narrator, and preparing setting. Uses examples from James, Balzac, Pater, Flaubert, etc.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scene should embody rather than state the appeal
rubrics_metrics.description: The important appeal or moral of a scene should be embodied in the scene's elements (setting, gestures, broken phrases) rather than announced as a statement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: As in the Susan Stringham—Densher scene: the appeal 'hangs in the air' and 'has not appeared as a statement or an announcement'; the cheerless room, falling light, uneasy movements, and broken phrases contribute so that 'one word is enough' when it comes. Aim to make the scene itself reveal the contour of the appeal; avoid explicit authorial announcement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use a narrator only when the narrator adds definite value
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not supply a seer/recorder (narrator) unless his presence 'is made a value in itself, contributing definitely to the effect of the subject.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For some subjects the narrator's voice is a positive asset (panoramic chronicle, generalized picture). But where the subject needs only to be reflected or pictured, a narrator may be dispensed with. Ask whether omniscience or commentary genuinely improves the work before invoking it.

rubrics_metrics.name: Match method to the subject (dramatic vs pictorial)
rubrics_metrics.description: Choose dramatic (scene/act-based) treatment for subjects that are essentially about action or a conspicuous situation; choose pictorial/narrative method when the subject requires a broad survey or generalized impression.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: The Awkward Age is a dramatic subject best rendered scenically; Thackeray-style chronicles (Esmond, The Virginians) are pictorial and require a narrator. Identify whether your subject is 'action essentially' or 'picture of a character/state of mind' and let that determine method.

rubrics_metrics.name: Render interior life through outward signs (looks, gestures)
rubrics_metrics.description: When possible, express thought and feeling by objective signs—telling looks, gestures, and speech—so that 'the process of thinking and feeling and seeing' is exposed to the reader.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For stories concerned with impact on mind (e.g., Strether), you can 'make use of these looks and gestures' and 'leave them to enact it.' This dramatization of thought lets the reader infer interior states without authorial exposition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintain methodological consistency
rubrics_metrics.description: If you commit to a method (e.g., pure drama), sustain it through the work; inconsistent switching between methods weakens effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Awkward Age is praised because 'everything is immediate and particular' and the author 'never once draws upon' narrative resources; such rigor is difficult but yields a homogeneous result. If you adopt a dominant method, resist gratuitous intrusions of others unless justified.

rubrics_metrics.name: Economy of means—prefer direct view when other things are equal
rubrics_metrics.description: When a direct, dramatic view of the matter is adequate, it is often the most economical and effective choice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The direct scene often renders the subject best 'where other things are equal.' Use direct dramatization rather than explanatory narration unless the narrator contributes something essential.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognize drama's limitation in conveying background and atmosphere
rubrics_metrics.description: The purely dramatic form is narrow in scope and can struggle to express the wider background, atmosphere, or outlying associations of the scene.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Drama is vivid and compact but 'can have no great depth' of background colour. If the effect depends on time, place, or social texture, dramatic presentation may need supplementation by pictorial/narrative description.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use setting/background deliberately to prepare and propel action
rubrics_metrics.description: Where background is essential, accumulate and 'mass' setting details so that when action begins the scene carries propulsive force.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Balzac's technique: mass the Maison Vauquer and provincial towns so the story, when reached, benefits immediately from a fully created impression. Consider deliberate, economical background-building to feed the drama.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid using an omniscient narrator for authorial convenience
rubrics_metrics.description: Do not resort to omniscient explanation merely because it is easier for the author; prefer making characters' doings expressive enough to require no comment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text warns of a 'showman' narrator who 'comes forward...without doing the story any particular service.' If exposition is serving only the author's convenience, rethink whether the scene itself can answer the reader's questions.

rubrics_metrics.name: For subjects of gradual inner change, allow for reflective/narrative treatment
rubrics_metrics.description: Stories emphasizing slow internal reverberation or complex shifts of consciousness may need narration/retrospect rather than pure drama to be fully apprehended.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Madame Bovary, The Ambassadors, Strether—these focus on changes of mind and may require a narrator to project the working of imagination over time; pure dramatization might fail to 'bring out all that it has to give.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Leverage the novelist's power to fix manner and speech
rubrics_metrics.description: A novelist can control not only words but the manner in which they are spoken—providing the best 'acting' and avoiding interpretive chance of the stage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When treating scenes dramatically, use authorial stage-direction and phrasing to set the ideal manner of speech and action, an advantage over the playwright who must trust actors' interpretations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider scope (time/space/crowds) when choosing method
rubrics_metrics.description: If the subject's temporal or spatial reach, or number of incidents/characters, exceeds the capacity of straight drama, prefer pictorial/narrative method.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Large, loose, manifold subjects (chronicles, many-crowded novels) 'exceed the capacity of the straight and dramatic method' and require the narrator's generalizing survey to keep the material coherent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dramatize undramatic subjects where possible but beware of loss
rubrics_metrics.description: An undramatic subject can often be rendered dramatically (via gestures, looks) to good effect, but this is an art and may not always be appropriate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The author recommends experimenting with dramatization of thought (the 'vision of a vision'), yet cautions that James's idiosyncratic methods can be mistaken for personal quirks. Apply this device judiciously and ensure the dramatization actually serves the subject.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be willing to experiment but justify departures from the 'easy way'
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors often default to narration because it is easier; when rejecting the easy pictorial summary for the harder dramatic method, do so only with clear cause and aim.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The text notes that treating a subject with 'the rigour of Henry James' is difficult and therefore rare. A deliberate tour de force (pure drama or pure subjectivity) can be valuable, but must be undertaken with awareness of the challenges and losses involved.
